lesson.title: Making Sense of Data: Mean, Median, Mode, and Spread
lesson.summary: Descriptive statistics summarize a whole data set with a small number of values, one describing the center and another describing how spread out the data is, and the ACT expects you to compute and interpret both.
lesson.body:
When you are handed a list of numbers, the first instinct is usually to ask what a typical value looks like. That is the job of a measure of center, and there are three common ones. The mean, or average, is the sum of all the values divided by how many values there are. The median is the middle value once the data is sorted from smallest to largest, if there is an odd number of values, the median is the single middle one, and if there is an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle ones. The mode is whichever value appears most often, a data set can have one mode, more than one mode if there is a tie, or no mode if every value is unique.

Center alone does not tell the whole story, though, since two very different data sets can share the same mean. That is where measures of spread come in. The range is the simplest, the largest value minus the smallest value. A more refined measure is the standard deviation, which describes on average how far each data point sits from the mean. To find it, subtract the mean from every value to get each value's deviation, square each deviation so that negative and positive differences do not cancel out, average those squared deviations to get the variance, and finally take the square root of the variance to bring the units back to match the original data. That final square root step is exactly the radical operation from two chapters ago.

Work through all of these measures on the data set 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9, which has 8 values. The mean is the sum divided by 8: 2+4+4+4+5+5+7+9 equals 40, and 40 divided by 8 is 5. The data is already sorted, and with 8 values (an even count) the median is the average of the 4th and 5th values, which are 4 and 5, giving a median of 4.5. The mode is 4, since it appears three times, more than any other value. The range is the largest value minus the smallest, 9 minus 2, which is 7.

Now find the standard deviation of that same set. The mean was 5, so subtract 5 from each value to get the deviations: -3, -1, -1, -1, 0, 0, 2, 4. Square each deviation: 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16. Add those squares: 9+1+1+1+0+0+4+16 equals 32. Divide by 8 to get the variance: 32 divided by 8 is 4. Take the square root to get the standard deviation: the square root of 4 is 2. So this data set has a mean of 5 and a standard deviation of 2, meaning values typically sit about 2 units away from the mean, which matches the spread you can see just by looking at the list.

The ACT often asks how a data set's mean, median, or standard deviation changes when a value is added, removed, or altered, rather than asking you to compute everything from scratch. Understanding what each measure actually represents, center versus spread, makes those reasoning questions far faster than recomputing every statistic by hand.
